What history is:
The study of the human past from the evidence it left behind — and the first thing to learn is that those are two different things.

**The past is everything that happened.** It is gone. Nobody can visit it, and almost all of it left no trace at all: most people who have ever lived are not recorded anywhere, by name or otherwise.

**History is what we can say about the past from what survives.** A letter, a coin, a burnt layer in the soil, a tax list, a skeleton, a ruined wall, a song still sung. The historian's work is to gather that evidence, test it, and build the most honest account it will support.

**The word itself says so.** *Historía* is Greek for **inquiry** — finding out by asking. Herodotus used it in the 430s BC for his book on the wars between the Greeks and Persia, and it is why he is called the father of history. History began as a method before it was a subject.

**What history is not:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Memory** | what a people tells itself about its past. Useful evidence, but it is shaped by what the teller needs now |
| **Heritage** | the past used to give a group an identity. Often moving; rarely complete |
| **Myth** | a story that explains the world. It can carry real memories inside it, but it is not checked against evidence |
| **Prophecy** | history does not repeat on a schedule, and it predicts nothing reliably |

**Three habits run through this whole curriculum:**

1. **Ask how we know.** Every claim rests on some evidence. A good lesson says what it is.
2. **Put things in their own time.** People in the past did not know how their story ended, and they did not think in our categories. Judging them is allowed; understanding them comes first.
3. **Look at the whole world at once.** What was happening in China while Rome rose? In West Africa while the Crusades were fought? The survey is built so each age is seen across every region.

**Prehistory and history.** By convention, **"history" in the narrow sense begins with writing**, around 3200 BC in Mesopotamia and Egypt, and everything before is **prehistory**. The line is a convenience, not a wall: prehistory is studied from bones, tools, pollen, DNA and the ground itself, and the first lessons of this stage are about exactly that.
The world at a glance:
Before anything happens, it has to happen somewhere. This lesson is the map every later lesson hangs on.

**Seven continents, but history uses regions.** Historians group the world by how people actually connected — by seas, rivers, deserts and mountain walls — more than by continent.

| Region | What shapes it |
| --- | --- |
| **The Near East** (Mesopotamia, the Levant, Anatolia, Iran) | two great rivers, the Tigris and Euphrates; the crossroads of three continents |
| **Egypt and North-East Africa** | the Nile, a ribbon of fertile land through desert; the Red Sea |
| **The Mediterranean** | an inland sea joining southern Europe, North Africa and the Levant |
| **Europe north of the Alps** | forests, rivers flowing to the Atlantic and Baltic, cold winters |
| **South Asia** (India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka) | the Indus and the Ganges; the Himalaya to the north; the monsoon |
| **East Asia** (China, Korea, Japan) | the Yellow and Yangtze rivers; deserts and steppe to the west; the Pacific |
| **The steppe** (from Hungary to Mongolia) | a belt of grassland across Eurasia — the highway of horse peoples |
| **Sub-Saharan Africa** | the Sahara as a sea of sand to cross; the Sahel, the forest, the great lakes, the south |
| **The Indian Ocean world** | a sea crossed by monsoon winds, joining East Africa, Arabia, India and South-East Asia |
| **The Americas** | Mesoamerica (Mexico and Central America), the Andes, the Amazon, North America; cut off from Eurasia until 1492 |
| **Oceania** | Australia, New Guinea, and the Pacific islands settled last of all |

**Three geographical facts that explain a great deal:**

1. **Eurasia is wide, not tall.** It runs east to west, so crops, animals and ideas could spread along the same latitudes, through similar climates. The Americas and Africa run north to south, across climate zones, which made the same spread harder. This argument is most associated with Jared Diamond; it is influential and also debated.
2. **Rivers make the first states.** Every early civilisation grew on a river that flooded and fed farmland: the Tigris-Euphrates, the Nile, the Indus, the Yellow River.
3. **Seas join; mountains and deserts divide.** The Mediterranean and the Indian Ocean were highways long before roads were. The Sahara, the Himalaya and the open Pacific were barriers that only certain technologies crossed.

**Two maps lie, and you should know how.** The common world map (the Mercator projection, 1569) was made for sailors and keeps compass directions true, at the cost of **swelling everything near the poles**: Greenland looks the size of Africa, which is in fact about **fourteen times larger**. Keep that in mind whenever a map makes Europe look large.
Evidence: primary and secondary sources:
Everything a historian says rests on sources. They come in two kinds, and the difference is the most useful idea in the subject.

**A primary source comes from the time being studied.** A letter written in 1916 from the trenches. A Roman coin. A tax list from the Ming dynasty. A temple inscription. A photograph. A skeleton. It is the raw evidence.

**A secondary source is written later, about that time**, using primary sources. A history book, a documentary, this lesson. It is an interpretation.

**The line is about use, not age.** Herodotus is a secondary source on the Trojan War, which happened centuries before him, and a primary source on how Greeks of the 400s BC saw the world.

**Primary sources are not automatically true.** Each was made by someone, for a reason. So a historian asks the same questions of every one:

| Question | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| **Who made it?** | a king's victory inscription and a soldier's letter see the same battle differently |
| **When, and how long after the event?** | memory fades and gets rewritten |
| **For whom?** | a speech to a crowd, a private diary and a tax record are written to be believed by different people |
| **Why?** | to boast, to persuade, to record, to sell, to pray |
| **What does it leave out?** | silences are evidence too |

**Kinds of evidence beyond writing:**

- **Archaeology** — buildings, tools, rubbish pits, graves. It records ordinary life that writers ignored.
- **Science** — DNA, pollen, ice cores, tree rings, isotopes in teeth that show where someone grew up.
- **Oral tradition** — histories kept by memory and performance, like the West African griots' epic of Sundiata. Easy to dismiss, and often surprisingly exact on some points.
- **Language** — related words across languages trace migrations no one wrote down.

**Corroboration is the rule.** One source is a claim. Two independent sources that agree are evidence. A source confirmed by archaeology or science is better still. Throughout this curriculum, when something rests on a single source, the lesson will say so.
Primary source: Herodotus says why he wr:
The opening sentence of the first history book in the Western tradition, read slowly.

**The text** (Herodotus, *Histories*, opening; written about 430 BC; translated by G. C. Macaulay, 1890):

> "This is the Showing forth of the Inquiry of Herodotus of Halicarnassos, to the end that neither the deeds of men may be forgotten by lapse of time, nor the works great and marvellous, which have been produced some by Hellenes and some by Barbarians, may lose their renown; and especially that the causes may be remembered for which these waged war with one another."

**Who.** Herodotus was born around 484 BC in Halicarnassus, a Greek city on the coast of what is now Turkey, then under Persian rule. He travelled widely — Egypt, the Black Sea, Babylon by his own account — and collected stories everywhere he went.

**Read it phrase by phrase:**

| Phrase | What it tells you |
| --- | --- |
| **"Inquiry"** (*historíē*) | the method: he asked, he looked, he compared |
| **"neither the deeds of men may be forgotten"** | the first purpose of history: memory against time |
| **"some by Hellenes and some by Barbarians"** | he means to credit both sides. *Barbarians* meant simply non-Greek speakers, and much of his book admires Persians and Egyptians |
| **"especially that the causes may be remembered"** | the second, larger purpose: **not just what happened but why** |

**That last clause is the birth of the subject.** Earlier records listed kings and victories. Herodotus asked what caused a war, and set out to answer from evidence.

**His weaknesses, which he partly admits.** He reports stories he does not believe ("I am bound to tell what is told, but not to believe it all"), some of his numbers are impossible (he gives Xerxes' army as over five million), and he sometimes trusted guides who invented things. Later Greeks called him the "father of lies" as well as the father of history.

**What to take from him.** The questions are still the right ones: what happened, why, and how do we know? The next lesson is the first of the tools for answering the last of them.
Counting years: BC, AD, BCE and CE:
Every date in this curriculum uses one counting system. It is worth knowing where it came from.

**The system: years counted from the birth of Christ.** It was worked out in **AD 525** by **Dionysius Exiguus**, a monk in Rome, to calculate the date of Easter. He replaced a count from the reign of the Roman emperor Diocletian, a persecutor of Christians.

**Two labels:**
- **AD** — *Anno Domini*, "in the year of the Lord": AD 1066.
- **BC** — "before Christ": 44 BC. Years BC count **down** towards the birth: 500 BC is earlier than 400 BC.

**The Venerable Bede**, an English monk, spread it by using it in his *Ecclesiastical History of the English People* (731), and from there it became the standard of Western Europe, and later of the world.

**There is no year zero.** The year before AD 1 is 1 BC. So the span from 1 BC to AD 1 is one year, and the "third millennium" strictly began in 2001.

**BCE and CE** — "before the common era" and "common era" — are **the same numbers with different labels**, used by many historians and scientists as religiously neutral. 44 BC is 44 BCE. This curriculum uses **BC and AD**.

**Dionysius probably got the birth wrong.** Herod the Great, who the Gospels say was alive at Christ's birth, died around 4 BC, so the Nativity is usually placed around **6–4 BC**. The count stands anyway: it is a convention, not a claim.

**Other ways of counting years, which you will meet:**

| Calendar | Counted from |
| --- | --- |
| Roman (*AUC*) | the founding of Rome, traditionally 753 BC |
| Byzantine | the creation of the world, set at 5509 BC |
| Islamic (*AH*) | the Hijra, Muhammad's journey to Medina, AD 622; lunar years, so shorter |
| Chinese | the reigns of emperors, each with its own era name |
| Jewish | the creation, set at 3761 BC |

**Two words for long spans:** a **century** is a hundred years — the 5th century BC is 500–401 BC; the 19th century AD is the 1800s. **BP**, "before present", is used for very old dates, where "present" is fixed at 1950.
Dating without writing: layers, tree rin:
Most of the human past has no written dates. These are the three methods that supply them.

**1. Stratigraphy: the layer cake.** Soil, rubbish and ruins build up over time, **newer on top of older**. An object in a lower layer is usually older than one above it. This gives **relative dating** — what came before what — but not years.

Disturbances spoil it: a pit dug through layers, a burrowing animal, a flood. Excavators record every layer so these can be spotted.

**2. Dendrochronology: tree rings.** A tree grows one ring a year, wide in good years and thin in bad ones. The pattern of wide and narrow rings is the same across trees in one region, so it can be **matched from living trees back into old timbers**, building one continuous record. In Europe that record now reaches back about **12,000 years**. A beam from a medieval roof can be dated to the year its tree was felled.

**3. Radiocarbon dating — the great one.** Worked out by **Willard Libby** in the late 1940s; he won the Nobel Prize for it in 1960.

- Living things take in carbon, including a tiny, steady share of radioactive **carbon-14**.
- When they die, they stop. The carbon-14 then decays at a fixed rate: **half of it is gone after about 5,730 years** (its half-life).
- Measure how much is left in bone, wood, charcoal or cloth, and you know how long ago it died.

**Its limits:** it only works on things that were once alive; it reaches back about **50,000 years**, after which too little is left; and the raw result must be **calibrated** against tree rings, because the amount of carbon-14 in the air has varied. A good date is given as a range: "3200–3100 BC".

**Further back, other clocks:** rocks and volcanic ash are dated by the decay of potassium into argon, which reaches millions of years — this is how the first human ancestors in East Africa are dated, by the ash layers above and below them. And **DNA** gives a different kind of clock: by counting differences between populations, geneticists estimate when they split apart.

**Why this matters for history.** Before about 1950, the dates of prehistory were educated guesses. Radiocarbon changed them, often by thousands of years — and showed, for example, that some monuments in western Europe were **older** than the pyramids, not copies of them.
Why things happen: cause, consequence an:
Herodotus wanted "the causes". This lesson is about how historians actually think about them.

**Most events have many causes, of different kinds.** Take the outbreak of the First World War in 1914:

| Kind | Example |
| --- | --- |
| **Long-term** (structural) | alliances that tied the great powers together; an arms race; nationalism |
| **Short-term** | a crisis in the Balkans; Austria-Hungary's ultimatum to Serbia |
| **Trigger** | the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo, 28 June 1914 |

**The trigger is not the cause.** Archdukes had been threatened before without a world war. The question is why *this* shot started *that* war — which is a question about the long-term causes.

**Three things historians weigh:**

1. **Structures** — geography, climate, economics, technology, disease. Slow forces that set what is possible.
2. **Choices** — what particular people decided. Structures do not act; people do.
3. **Chance** — contingency. Weather, an illness, a message that arrived late. History is full of moments that could have gone the other way.

**Consequences, and unintended ones.** Every event has effects nobody planned. The Europeans who crossed the Atlantic in 1492 did not intend to kill most of the population of the Americas, but the diseases they carried did exactly that. Intended results are usually the smallest part of what happens.

**Two traps to avoid:**
- **Hindsight.** Because we know how things ended, the ending looks inevitable. It rarely was. People at the time faced an open future.
- **The single cause.** "Rome fell because of lead pipes" or "because of Christianity" — one-cause answers are almost always wrong. Edward Gibbon counted many causes, and modern historians count more.

**A good question to ask of every event in this curriculum:** what made it possible, what made it likely, and what made it happen then?
When historians disagree:
History is not settled once and for all. Knowing why historians disagree is how you read them well.

**They disagree for good reasons:**

1. **New evidence turns up.** A shipwreck, a buried archive, a DNA study. The arrival of ancient DNA after 2010 rewrote the story of European prehistory in under a decade.
2. **They ask different questions.** A military historian and an economic historian looking at the same war will notice different things.
3. **The evidence is thin or one-sided.** Where only one side wrote, the other side's story must be reconstructed, and reconstructions differ.
4. **Their own times shape them.** Every generation brings its own concerns to the past. That is not bias in the bad sense; it is why history is rewritten.

**A famous example: why did the Western Roman Empire fall?** Over two hundred causes have been proposed. The main schools:

| Reading | The argument |
| --- | --- |
| **Decline from within** (Gibbon, 1776–1789) | corruption, loss of civic virtue, the army's power, and — controversially — Christianity |
| **Murder from outside** | the Germanic and Hunnic invasions destroyed a working state |
| **Transformation** (from the 1970s) | it did not "fall" so much as change into the medieval world; continuity mattered more than collapse |
| **Collapse after all** (Bryan Ward-Perkins, 2005) | archaeology shows real catastrophe: smaller cattle, cruder pottery, fewer coins — living standards fell sharply |

**Each has evidence.** The question is which evidence weighs most, and that is where the argument lives.

**How this curriculum handles it.** Where historians genuinely disagree, a lesson gives **the strongest form of each reading** and **what evidence would settle it**, rather than choosing for you. Where they agree, the lesson says so plainly. And where the record is simply too thin to know, it says that too.

**Revisionism is normal.** "Revisionist" is sometimes used as an insult, but all good history is revision. The line that matters is between **revising from evidence** and **denying evidence** — the difference between a historian and a propagandist.
Deep time: the Earth and the first homin:
To place humans, start with how short our part of the story is.

**The scale:**

| | Years ago |
| --- | --- |
| The Earth forms | about **4.54 billion** |
| The first life (single cells) | about **3.7–3.5 billion** |
| Animals in the sea | about **540 million** |
| The dinosaurs die out | **66 million** |
| Our line splits from chimpanzees' | about **7–6 million** |
| *Homo sapiens* appears | about **300,000** |
| Farming begins | about **11,500** |
| Writing | about **5,200** |

**Squeeze the Earth's history into one day** and modern humans arrive in the last **six seconds** before midnight. All of written history fits in the last tenth of a second.

**What a hominin is.** Humans and our extinct relatives after the split from the chimpanzee line. Chimpanzees and bonobos are our **closest living relatives**, sharing about **98–99%** of our DNA, but we did not descend from them: we share a common ancestor.

**The earliest candidates**, all from Africa:
- ***Sahelanthropus*** (Chad, about 7 million years ago) — a skull with features suggesting it may have walked upright.
- ***Orrorin*** (Kenya, about 6 million).
- ***Ardipithecus*** (Ethiopia, about 4.4 million) — "Ardi", a partial skeleton showing a creature that climbed trees and also walked on two legs.

How many of these are truly our ancestors, rather than cousins, is **debated**: the fossils are few and fragmentary.

**Why Africa.** Every early hominin fossil comes from Africa, and the genetic evidence agrees. For most of human evolution, **Africa was the whole human world**. The Great Rift Valley of East Africa, with its volcanic ash layers that can be dated, and the limestone caves of South Africa, which preserve bones well, are where most of the evidence has been found.

**A warning about the "march of progress".** The famous picture of an ape becoming a man in a single line is wrong. Human evolution is a **branching bush**: many hominin species lived, several at the same time, and most were dead ends.
Standing up: the australopithecines:
Before big brains or tools, our ancestors did one decisive thing: they walked on two legs.

**Who.** The **australopithecines** ("southern apes"), a group of hominins living in eastern and southern Africa from about **4.2 to 2 million years ago**. Ape-sized brains, ape-like faces, and a human way of walking.

**Lucy.** The most famous fossil in the world: a partial skeleton of ***Australopithecus afarensis***, found at **Hadar, Ethiopia, in 1974** by Donald Johanson's team, dated about **3.2 million years ago**. About 40% of one individual, a little over a metre tall. Her pelvis and knee show **she walked upright**; her long arms and curved fingers show she still climbed. (She was named after the Beatles' "Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds", playing in the camp that night.)

**The Laetoli footprints.** In Tanzania, about **3.66 million years ago**, hominins walked across wet volcanic ash that then hardened. Found in 1978 by Mary Leakey's team, the trail is unmistakably **upright, two-footed walking** — the oldest direct evidence of it.

**The Taung Child.** In **1924**, at Taung in South Africa, the anatomist **Raymond Dart** described the skull of a young child, naming the species ***Australopithecus africanus***. He argued it was a human ancestor and that **Africa was the cradle of humankind**. Most scientists rejected this for decades — they expected human origins in Europe or Asia — until more finds proved him right. South Africa's "Cradle of Humankind" near Johannesburg is now a World Heritage Site for exactly this reason.

**Why walk upright?** Still debated. Leading ideas:
- it frees the hands to carry food and infants;
- it is efficient for walking long distances across open country;
- it keeps less of the body in the sun in hot grassland.
Probably several of these together, as forests in East Africa broke up into mixed woodland and grass.

**The other branch.** Alongside the slender australopithecines lived the "robust" ***Paranthropus***, with huge jaws and teeth for chewing tough plants, which lasted until about 1.2 million years ago — another dead end on the bush.
The first tools:
The moment our ancestors started shaping stone is the start of technology, and of the archaeological record.

**The Oldowan.** Named after Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania, where Louis and Mary Leakey found them in the 1930s onwards. Simple tools made by **striking one stone against another** to knock off sharp flakes. The oldest are about **2.6 million years old**, from Gona in Ethiopia.

**They were used to butcher.** Animal bones from the same sites carry **cut marks** and are smashed open for marrow. Early hominins were eating meat — probably scavenged from the kills of lions and other predators as much as hunted.

**Older still?** In 2015, tools from **Lomekwi in Kenya** were dated to about **3.3 million years ago**, before the genus *Homo* is known. If they hold up — some researchers question the dating — then tools were invented by australopithecines, not by us.

***Homo habilis*, "handy man".** Named by Louis Leakey and colleagues in 1964 for the toolmaker of Olduvai, about **2.4–1.6 million years ago**. A larger brain than the australopithecines', and the first species placed in our own genus, *Homo*. Its status is argued over; some think it belongs with the australopithecines.

**The Acheulean hand-axe.** From about **1.76 million years ago**, a new kind of tool appears: a **teardrop-shaped hand-axe**, worked on both faces into a deliberate, symmetrical form. Named after Saint-Acheul in France, where they were first described, but **far older in Africa**. It lasted, with little change, for over **a million years** — the most successful tool design in history.

**What the hand-axe tells us about minds.** To make one, a toolmaker must hold a shape in mind and work towards it through dozens of blows. That is **planning**, and it probably had to be **taught**, by showing — perhaps the beginnings of the social learning that culture depends on.

**Why stone survives and the rest does not.** Early hominins surely used wood, bone, fibre and leather too, but those rot. The archaeological record is biased towards stone, so the "Stone Age" is named after what lasted, not necessarily what mattered most.
Homo erectus and the first journeys out:
The first hominin to look, from the neck down, much like us — and the first to leave Africa.

**Who.** ***Homo erectus*** ("upright man"), from about **1.9 million years ago** to perhaps **110,000 years ago** in Java — the longest-lived human species known. Its African form is sometimes called *Homo ergaster*.

**The Turkana Boy.** A nearly complete skeleton of a youth, found at Lake Turkana, Kenya, in **1984**, about **1.6 million years old**. Long legs, a tall narrow body built for heat, and human body proportions: a **walker and runner of open country**, no longer a climber.

**A bigger brain, and a different life.** Brains grew to about two-thirds of ours. To feed that costly organ, *erectus* probably ate more meat and fat — and may have **cooked** (the next lesson). It made Acheulean hand-axes.

**Out of Africa, the first time.** *Homo erectus* spread across Asia remarkably early:

| Place | Find | Age |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Dmanisi, Georgia** | five skulls, small-brained, with simple tools | about **1.8 million years** |
| **Java, Indonesia** | "Java Man", found by Eugène Dubois in **1891** | over 1.5 million years |
| **Zhoukoudian, China** | "Peking Man", 1920s–30s (the original fossils were lost in 1941) | about **780,000–400,000** |

**How?** Probably not a planned migration but a slow spread, generation by generation, following game and grassland across the Middle East and Asia — a few kilometres a generation adds up to a continent in a few thousand years.

**The puzzle of Flores.** On the Indonesian island of Flores, stone tools about **one million years old** — and the bones of a later tiny hominin, ***Homo floresiensis*** ("the hobbit"), about a metre tall, alive until about **50,000 years ago**. Flores has always been an island. How did they get there? Rafting, drifting on vegetation after a storm, or something we do not yet understand.

**Why it matters.** For more than a million years, humans of one kind or another lived across Africa and Asia. Our own species was, much later, the **second wave** out of Africa — into a world that already had people in it.
Fire:
The control of fire changed what humans ate, how they lived together, and where they could live.

**Natural fire is everywhere** — lightning, volcanoes. The question is when hominins began to **keep and use it**, and later to **make** it at will.

**The evidence, oldest first:**

| Site | What was found | Age |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Wonderwerk Cave, South Africa** | burnt bone and plant ash deep inside a cave, where lightning could not reach | about **1 million years** |
| **Gesher Benot Ya'aqov, Israel** | burnt seeds, wood and flint around hearths | about **790,000 years** |
| **Qesem Cave, Israel** | a hearth used again and again | about **300,000 years** |

Claims for fire older than a million years exist (Kenya, about 1.5 million) but are **disputed**: it is hard to tell a campfire from a bush fire in such old ground. By about **400,000 years ago**, the evidence for regular fire use is clear in several places.

**What fire did:**

1. **Cooking.** Cooked food is softer and gives up more energy. The primatologist **Richard Wrangham** argues cooking is what allowed our big brains and small guts — a bold theory, still debated, but the effect of cooking on digestion is real.
2. **Warmth.** Fire made colder lands livable, and the night less dangerous.
3. **Protection.** Predators avoid fire. Sleeping on the ground became safer.
4. **Light, and time.** A fire extends the day. The hours around it became time for talk, teaching and story — possibly one of the places where language and culture grew.
5. **Tools.** Later humans used heat to harden wooden spears and to make stone easier to flake, as at Pinnacle Point in South Africa about 164,000 years ago.

**Making fire** — with flint and iron pyrite, or by friction of wood — is harder to detect than using it. The earliest good evidence comes from Neanderthal tools of about 50,000 years ago, worn in a way that suggests striking sparks.
Our cousins: Neanderthals, Denisovans an:
When our species appeared, we were not alone. For most of our history, several kinds of human shared the planet.

**Neanderthals** (*Homo neanderthalensis*). Named after the Neander Valley in Germany, where a skeleton was found in **1856**. They lived across **Europe and western Asia** from about **400,000 to about 40,000 years ago**.

- **Built for cold:** stocky, strong, with large noses and **brains as big as ours or bigger**.
- **Skilled:** fine stone tools, hunting of large animals at close range, use of fire, care for the injured — one man at Shanidar in Iraq survived for years with a withered arm and a blind eye.
- **Symbolic?** Probably: there is evidence of pigments, eagle-talon jewellery, and in Spain, cave markings dated to over 64,000 years ago, before modern humans arrived — though that dating is argued over. Whether they buried their dead with ceremony is also **debated**.

**The old picture of a brutish "caveman" is wrong.** It came from one arthritic old skeleton, reconstructed badly in 1911.

**Denisovans.** Known almost entirely **from DNA**. In **2010**, genes were read from a **finger bone** in Denisova Cave, Siberia, and turned out to belong to a human group no one had known about. A jawbone from Tibet and a few teeth have since been linked to them. They lived across Asia.

**And others:**
- ***Homo floresiensis*** on Flores (previous lesson).
- ***Homo luzonensis*** on Luzon, Philippines (described 2019).
- ***Homo naledi*** in South Africa's Rising Star cave system (described 2015): small-brained, yet living as late as **335,000–236,000 years ago**, alongside early *Homo sapiens*.

**We are partly them.** In **2010**, the Neanderthal genome showed that **people outside Africa carry about 1–2% Neanderthal DNA**, from interbreeding after our ancestors left Africa. Many people in Melanesia and Australia also carry Denisovan DNA. Some of these genes still affect immunity, skin and adaptation to altitude — Tibetans' tolerance of thin air comes partly from Denisovans.

**Why did they disappear?** By about **40,000 years ago** the Neanderthals are gone. Competition with modern humans, small and scattered populations, climate swings, and absorption by interbreeding are all proposed — **probably several together**. They did not vanish entirely: they are in us.
Homo sapiens in Africa:
Our own species, and where and when it began.

**The oldest fossils.** At **Jebel Irhoud in Morocco**, skulls and tools dated in **2017** to about **300,000 years ago** have a modern face and a longer, less rounded braincase. At **Omo Kibish in Ethiopia**, fossils first found in 1967 are about **230,000 years old**. At **Herto, Ethiopia**, skulls about **160,000 years old**.

**Not one Eden but a continent.** The finds are scattered from Morocco to Ethiopia to South Africa. Many researchers now think *Homo sapiens* emerged **across Africa**, from populations that met and mixed, rather than in one place. The modern rounded skull took shape gradually, by about 100,000 years ago.

**The genetic evidence agrees.** Living Africans hold **more genetic diversity than the rest of the world combined**: two people from different parts of Africa can differ more than a European and an East Asian. This is what you expect if humanity grew up in Africa and a small group later left. The deepest branches of the human family tree belong to the **San** and other peoples of southern Africa.

**What "modern" means.** Two kinds of modernity, which did not arrive together:
- **Anatomical** — the body and skull of a modern human, by about 300,000–100,000 years ago.
- **Behavioural** — symbols, art, ornaments, planned long-distance trade, complex tools. Long thought to appear suddenly about 50,000 years ago in Europe; **now seen to appear much earlier, and gradually, in Africa** (the next lesson).

**Life in a changing Africa.** The climate swung between wet and dry. During one long cold, dry period, about 190,000–130,000 years ago, human numbers may have fallen low, and the southern coast of Africa — with shellfish, plants and a milder climate — may have been one refuge. This is the argument of the archaeologist Curtis Marean, from his work at **Pinnacle Point** near Mossel Bay; it is influential and still debated.

**The key idea for the rest of the stage:** for about **two hundred thousand years**, all of us lived in Africa. Everything that followed — every people, every language, every civilisation — descends from those Africans.
The first symbols: Blombos and the beads:
The oldest evidence of a mind that thinks in symbols — the ability that makes language, art, money and religion possible — comes from the southern tip of Africa.

**Blombos Cave**, on the coast of the Western Cape, South Africa, excavated by **Christopher Henshilwood** from 1991.

**What was found there:**

| Find | Age | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Engraved ochre** — red iron-oxide stone with a cross-hatched pattern scratched on it | about **75,000–73,000 years** | a pattern made on purpose, with no practical use |
| **Shell beads** — tiny snail shells, pierced and worn smooth, some coloured with ochre | about **75,000 years** | ornaments worn on the body: a sign of identity, belonging or status |
| **A paint workshop** — two abalone shells used as containers to mix ochre, bone, charcoal and fat | about **100,000 years** | a recipe, followed in steps, to make paint |
| **A drawing** — a cross-hatched pattern drawn in ochre crayon on a flake of stone | about **73,000 years** | the oldest known drawing |

**Elsewhere in Africa:** pierced shell beads at **Taforalt in Morocco** and in Algeria and Israel about **82,000–100,000 years ago**; engraved ostrich eggshell water containers at **Diepkloof**, also in the Western Cape, about **60,000 years ago**.

**Why symbols matter more than tools.** A hand-axe is useful in itself. A bead is useful only because people **agree on what it means**. A culture of shared meanings is the beginning of everything that is distinctively human: language, ritual, law, art and trade.

**What the patterns meant, no one knows.** Decoration, a sign of a group, a tally, a record of something seen — they cannot be read. The point is that someone meant something by them.

**An argument settled — mostly.** Earlier archaeologists, working in Europe, thought a "human revolution" of art and symbols happened suddenly about 40,000–50,000 years ago. Blombos and the African finds showed **the roots were in Africa, tens of thousands of years earlier**, and grew gradually. Some still argue for a later threshold, but the African evidence is now the starting point of the debate.
Out of Africa: the great dispersal:
How our species came to live everywhere.

**Early attempts.** Modern humans reached the Middle East more than once: skulls from **Misliya in Israel** are about **180,000 years old**, and from **Apidima in Greece**, possibly 210,000 — though that one is contested. Most of these early groups seem to have **died out or retreated**. They left little or no trace in living people.

**The great dispersal: about 70,000–50,000 years ago.** The genetic evidence says that **almost everyone outside Africa descends from a small population that left Africa** in this window. Where they crossed is argued:

- **The northern route** — up the Nile and across Sinai into the Levant.
- **The southern route** — across the narrow strait of **Bab-el-Mandeb** at the mouth of the Red Sea into Arabia, when low sea levels made it easier, and then along the coasts of the Indian Ocean.

Both may have been used.

**How fast they spread:**

| Region | Modern humans present by about |
| --- | --- |
| The Middle East | 55,000 years ago |
| South Asia | 55,000–50,000 |
| South-East Asia and Australia | 50,000 (perhaps earlier) |
| Europe | **45,000** |
| East Asia | 45,000–40,000 |
| Siberia | 45,000 |
| The Americas | by 15,000 (perhaps much earlier) |

**Meeting the others.** They met Neanderthals in the Middle East and Europe, and Denisovans in Asia — and had children with them, as the DNA shows.

**A bottleneck.** The small size of the founding group explains why non-Africans are genetically **less diverse** than Africans: they carry only a sample of Africa's variety.

**Why then?** Probably a mix: climate windows that opened routes across deserts, growing populations, and perhaps the symbolic and social skills of the last lesson, which let people trade and cooperate across distance. **Not proven**; the dispersal is one of the great open questions.

**The result.** By about 40,000 years ago, our species was the only human left across most of Eurasia. By 12,000 years ago, on every continent but Antarctica.
The Ice Age world:
The world our ancestors spread across was not the world we know. It was colder, drier, and shaped differently.

**The Ice Age.** For the last 2.6 million years the Earth has swung between long cold **glacial** periods and short warm **interglacials**. Our species lived through more than one. The last glacial period peaked in the **Last Glacial Maximum**, about **26,000–20,000 years ago**.

**What it looked like at the peak:**

- **Ice sheets** up to three kilometres thick covered Canada, the northern United States, Scandinavia and Britain north of the Thames.
- **Sea levels were about 120 metres lower**, because so much water was locked in ice. Coastlines lay far out from today's.
- **Land bridges** joined Britain to Europe (the drowned plain called **Doggerland**), Siberia to Alaska (**Beringia**), and New Guinea to Australia (**Sahul**). The islands of Indonesia formed a peninsula of Asia (**Sunda**).
- Much of the world was **drier and windier**; the Sahara was larger, and rainforests shrank.

**The animals.** The **megafauna** — mammoths, woolly rhinoceroses, cave lions, giant deer, giant ground sloths in the Americas, giant kangaroos and marsupial lions in Australia. Most were gone by about 10,000 years ago. Whether **human hunting or climate change** killed them is a classic debate; the answer seems to differ by continent, and in Australia and the Americas the timing of their disappearance after humans arrived points strongly at us.

**How people lived in the cold.** In Ice Age Europe and Siberia, hunters followed herds of reindeer, horse and mammoth. They built huts from **mammoth bones and tusks** in Ukraine (Mezhyrich, about 15,000 years ago), sewed fitted clothing with **bone needles**, and made the great cave paintings (a later lesson).

**The lost coasts.** Because seas were lower, **the coastlines where people likely lived are now underwater**. Much of the evidence for coastal life and coastal migration is on the seabed — one reason the routes of the dispersal are hard to prove.

**The warming.** From about 19,000 years ago the ice began to retreat, with sudden cold snaps (the last, the **Younger Dryas**, about 12,900–11,700 years ago). Then the climate settled into the stable, warm period we still live in, the **Holocene**, from about **11,700 years ago** — the stable climate in which farming, and everything after it, became possible.
Into Australia and the Americas:
The two longest journeys of the dispersal: one across the sea, one across a vanished land.

**Australia.** Even with sea levels low, reaching Sahul — Australia and New Guinea joined — meant **crossing open water**, at least 70–100 kilometres at a stretch. These were the **first deliberate sea voyages** we know of, by boat or raft.

- **When:** people were certainly there by about **50,000 years ago**. The site of **Madjedbebe** in Arnhem Land gave dates of about **65,000 years** in 2017; these are debated, but if right they push the arrival back.
- **Lake Mungo**, New South Wales: the remains of "Mungo Man" and "Mungo Lady", about **42,000 years old**, the latter the oldest known cremation in the world.
- **The longest continuous culture.** The ancestors of Aboriginal Australians and Papuans have lived there ever since — the oldest continuous cultures on Earth. Aboriginal rock art includes paintings tens of thousands of years old.

**The Americas.** Here the route was by land, then along the coast. During the Ice Age, **Beringia** joined Siberia to Alaska, and people lived on it for thousands of years. Ice sheets then blocked the way south — until they melted or a coastal path opened.

**When people reached the Americas is one of the liveliest debates in prehistory:**

| Reading | Evidence |
| --- | --- |
| **"Clovis first"** (dominant in the 20th century) | fine stone spear points from about **13,000 years ago**, found across North America, after an ice-free corridor opened |
| **Pre-Clovis** (now widely accepted) | **Monte Verde, Chile**, about **14,500 years ago** — too far south and too early for Clovis to be first |
| **Much earlier** (debated) | human **footprints at White Sands, New Mexico**, dated to about **23,000–21,000 years ago** (2021, re-dated in 2023) — before the Last Glacial Maximum ended |

**What would settle it:** more sites with secure dates, especially along the drowned Pacific coast, and DNA from early remains. The genetics already shows that most Native Americans descend from a population that split from Siberians about **25,000–20,000 years ago**.

**The last places.** The remote Pacific islands — Hawaii, New Zealand, Easter Island — were settled only in the last 1,000–3,000 years by the Polynesians (a later stage). Antarctica was never settled at all.
How hunter-gatherers lived:
For about 95% of our species' history, every human lived by hunting, fishing and gathering. This is the life our bodies and minds were shaped for.

**What we know comes from two kinds of evidence:** archaeology (camps, bones, tools) and the study of recent hunter-gatherers — the **San** of the Kalahari, the **Hadza** of Tanzania, Aboriginal Australians, the Inuit. Recent peoples are not "living fossils" — they have their own long histories and live in marginal lands — but they show what such a life can be.

**The shape of the life:**

- **Small bands** of about **20–50 people**, part of a wider network of a few hundred to a thousand who met, married and traded.
- **Mobile**, moving with the seasons to where food was. Few possessions, because everything had to be carried.
- **A broad diet:** dozens of plants, shellfish, fish, insects, small and large game. In most groups studied, **gathered plant food supplied more calories than meat**.
- **Sharing.** Food — especially meat from a big kill — was shared widely. Sharing is insurance: the hunter who fails today eats from the one who succeeded.
- **Fairly equal.** No chiefs with power to command; leaders lead by persuasion. Boastful hunters are mocked down to size, as among the San.

**"The original affluent society"?** In **1966** the anthropologist **Marshall Sahlins** argued that hunter-gatherers worked only a few hours a day for their food and had much leisure — rich in time, if not in things. This was drawn partly from **Richard Lee's** study of the !Kung San. Later work found the hours were longer once food processing and making tools were counted. **The truth is in between**: not paradise, not misery.

**The hard parts.** High infant mortality, injury, and in some groups, high rates of violent death. Life expectancy at birth was low, mainly because so many children died; those who reached adulthood often lived into their sixties.

**Not all the same.** Some hunter-gatherers were not mobile at all. Where food was rich and reliable — the salmon rivers of the North American Pacific coast, for example — people lived in **permanent villages**, built large houses, held slaves and ranked themselves by wealth. Hunter-gatherers were as varied as farmers would be.

**Why it matters for what comes next.** Farming, which the next stage begins with, was not an obvious improvement. Early farmers often worked harder, ate a narrower diet and were shorter and less healthy than the hunter-gatherers before them. Why people farmed anyway is one of the big questions of history.
Cave art and the first figurines:
The first great works of human imagination, and what we can and cannot say about them.

**The oldest painted pictures are in Indonesia.** On the island of **Sulawesi**, cave paintings of animals and hand stencils have been dated by the mineral crusts over them: a painting of wild pigs at Leang Tedongnge to at least **45,500 years ago**, and a scene of human-like figures and a pig at Leang Karampuang to at least **51,200 years** (published 2024). These upset the old idea that art began in Europe.

**The great caves of Europe:**

| Cave | Age | What is there |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Chauvet**, France (found 1994) | about **36,000 years** | lions, rhinoceroses, horses, bears, drawn with shading and perspective |
| **Lascaux**, France (found 1940 by teenagers) | about **17,000 years** | some 600 paintings: aurochs, horses, deer; one mysterious bird-headed man |
| **Altamira**, Spain (recognised 1880) | about **36,000–15,000 years** | painted bison on the ceiling — dismissed as a forgery when first reported, because no one believed "primitives" could paint like that |

**Carving and music.** In south-western Germany, about **40,000 years ago**:
- the **Lion-Man of Hohlenstein-Stadel** — a figure with a man's body and a lion's head, carved from mammoth ivory: an imagined being, not a copy of anything seen;
- the **Venus of Hohle Fels** — the oldest known figure of a human, a woman with exaggerated breasts and hips;
- **flutes** of bird bone and ivory: the oldest known musical instruments.

**What it meant: the honest answer is that we do not know.** The main readings:
- **Hunting magic** — painting animals to bring success in the hunt. But the animals painted are often not the ones eaten.
- **Shamanism** — the images record visions in trance. The South African archaeologist **David Lewis-Williams** built this reading from the rock art of the **San**, whose descendants could explain some of its meanings; it is powerful and contested when applied to Europe.
- **Storytelling, teaching, marking territory, or art for its own sake.** Probably meanings differed between places and across tens of thousands of years.

**What is certain.** People went deep into dark caves, by the light of fat lamps, to make these images. They had the same imagination and skill as any later artist. **The minds that painted Chauvet were fully our own.**
Connections: the world at the end of the:
The stage closes where the next one opens: about **12,000 years ago**, just before farming. Here is the human world at that moment.

**Where people lived.** On every continent but Antarctica. Perhaps **a few million people** in all — estimates range from about one to ten million — fewer than live in a single large city today.

**How they lived.** Everywhere, by hunting, fishing and gathering. But not everywhere the same way:

| Region | Life around 12,000 years ago |
| --- | --- |
| **The Levant** | the **Natufians**: hunter-gatherers living in villages of stone houses, harvesting wild cereals with sickles — on the edge of farming |
| **Ice-free Europe** | reindeer and horse hunters, following the herds north as the ice retreated |
| **Japan** | the **Jōmon**, making some of the world's **oldest pottery** (over 15,000 years old), long before farming |
| **China** | pottery fragments about **20,000 years old** at Xianrendong Cave, used by hunter-gatherers |
| **Africa** | the Sahara turning green and wet; people fishing in great lakes where there is now desert |
| **Australia** | Aboriginal peoples across the whole continent, with many hundreds of languages |
| **The Americas** | new arrivals spreading south fast, hunting the last mammoths and giant sloths |

**What connected them.** Not empires or trade routes yet, but:
- **Exchange networks** — shells, obsidian and ochre carried hundreds of kilometres, hand to hand.
- **Shared ways of making** tools and art across wide areas.
- **Kin and marriage** between neighbouring bands.

**What had already been achieved.** Symbols and art, music, boats and the crossing of seas, sewn clothing, the bow (in Africa, perhaps 60,000 years ago), the domestic **dog** (tamed from wolves, probably in Eurasia, at least 15,000 years ago), pottery in East Asia, and settled villages in the richest places.

**What was about to change.** As the Holocene's stable warmth arrived, people in several places began — independently — to **plant crops and keep animals**. That is the subject of Stage 2, and it is the most important change in how humans lived until the industrial revolution.

**Look back at the whole stage:** history is built from evidence; the evidence for most of the human story is in the ground, in bones and in genes; and for nearly all of it, all of us were hunter-gatherers whose ancestors came out of Africa.
